title: Workspaces
intro: Workspaces let one configuration keep several independent state files — a quick way to spin up isolated copies of the same infrastructure.

steps.explanation: The * marks the currently selected workspace.
steps.why: Every Terraform project starts in 'default'. Always know which workspace you're in before applying — they share code but not state.

steps.prompt: Create a new workspace for a short-lived feature test environment called 'feature-login'.
steps.fake_output:
Created and switched to workspace "feature-login"!

You're now on a new, empty workspace.
steps.explanation: A brand new, empty state — applying here builds a completely separate copy of everything.
steps.why: This is the strongest use case for workspaces: temporary, disposable copies of an environment for testing a branch, torn down afterward.

steps.prompt: Confirm which workspace is active before applying anything.
steps.explanation: Prints just the current workspace name.
steps.why: Your config can reference it as terraform.workspace, e.g. naming resources "app-${terraform.workspace}" so copies don't collide. Many teams also add it to their shell prompt to avoid applying in the wrong one.

steps.prompt: Testing's done and you've destroyed its resources. Switch back to staging.
steps.explanation: Subsequent plans and applies now use staging's state.
steps.why: Forgetting to switch back is the classic workspace accident: the next apply meant for staging goes to a different state entirely.

steps.explanation: Terraform refuses to delete a workspace whose state still has resources, unless forced.
steps.why: That refusal is a safety net: deleting a non-empty workspace would orphan real, still-running (still-billing) infrastructure with no state tracking it. Many teams prefer separate directories or separate backend configs over workspaces for dev/staging/prod precisely because it's harder to mix them up.
